statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a projective morphism of smooth quasi-projective [varieties](c:algebraic-variety) over an algebraically closed field. Then $\mathrm{ch}(f_! x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_Y) = f_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X))$ in $A(Y) \otimes \mathbb Q$ for every $x \in K_0(X)$, where $\mathrm{ch}$ is the [Chern character](c:chern-character), $\mathrm{td}$ the [Todd class](c:todd-class), $A$ the [Chow ring](c:chow-group) and $f_! = \sum_i (-1)^i R^i f_*$.

hypotheses.text: The morphism $f\colon X \to Y$ is projective.
The [varieties](c:algebraic-variety) $X$ and $Y$ are smooth and quasi-projective over an algebraically closed field.

conclusion: The [Chern character](c:chern-character) times the [Todd class](c:todd-class) commutes with pushforward: $\mathrm{ch}(f_! x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_Y) = f_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X))$.

proofs.name: Embedding and projection
proofs.slogan: Factor the morphism into a closed embedding and a projection from a projective bundle, prove the formula for each, and compose.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the embedding case of step 4 rests on the cited work. The case where $Y$ is a point is the Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem.

roles.why: Projectivity gives the factorization of $f$ through $\mathbb P^n \times Y$.
Smoothness gives tangent bundles, Todd classes, Chow rings and finite resolutions on every space of the proof.

steps.slogan: Factor $f$ as a closed embedding $i$ into $\mathbb P^n \times Y$ followed by the projection $p$.
steps.detail: A projective morphism factors as $f = p \circ i$, with $i$ a [closed immersion](c:is-closed-immersion) into $P = \mathbb P^n \times Y$ and $p$ the projection to $Y$. The space $P$ is smooth because $Y$ is smooth, so both factors are morphisms of smooth varieties.

steps.slogan: Show that the formula for $h$ and for $g$ gives the formula for $g \circ h$.
steps.detail: The maps $f_!$ on $K_0$ and $f_*$ on Chow rings are functorial: $(g h)_! = g_! h_!$ and $(g h)_* = g_* h_*$. The formula for $h\colon X \to Z$ replaces $\mathrm{td}(T_X)$ by $\mathrm{td}(T_Z)$, and the formula for $g\colon Z \to Y$ then replaces $\mathrm{td}(T_Z)$ by $\mathrm{td}(T_Y)$.

steps.slogan: Prove the formula for the projection $p\colon \mathbb P^n \times Y \to Y$ on generators.
steps.detail: $K_0(\mathbb P^n \times Y)$ is generated over $K_0(Y)$ by the classes $\mathcal O(k)$, and both sides are $K_0(Y)$-linear by the projection formula. For $p^*y \otimes \mathcal O(k)$ both sides equal $\binom{n+k}{n}\,\mathrm{ch}(y)\,\mathrm{td}(T_Y)$, by the residue computation of $\int_{\mathbb P^n} e^{kh}\,(h/(1 - e^{-h}))^{n+1}$.

steps.slogan: Prove the formula for the closed embedding $i$ with the Koszul complex of the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle).
steps.detail: The cited work reduces the embedding to the zero section of the normal bundle $N$ of $X$ in $P$. There the Koszul resolution gives $\mathrm{ch}(\lambda_{-1} N^\vee) = c_{\mathrm{top}}(N)\,\mathrm{td}(N)^{-1}$, and with $\mathrm{td}(T_X) = i^*\mathrm{td}(T_P)\,\mathrm{td}(N)^{-1}$ this yields $\mathrm{ch}(i_! x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_P) = i_*(\mathrm{ch}(x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X))$.

steps.slogan: Compose the two cases to get the formula for $f = p \circ i$.
steps.detail: Step 2 applies to $h = i$ and $g = p$, whose formulas come from steps 4 and 3. So the [Chern character](c:chern-character) times the [Todd class](c:todd-class) commutes with $f_!$ and $f_*$.

concepts.c:algebraic-variety: The formula relates the smooth varieties $X$ and $Y$ along $f$.
concepts.c:chern-character: The Chern character turns K-theory classes into rational Chow classes.
concepts.c:todd-class: The Todd class is the correction factor that makes pushforwards commute.
concepts.c:chow-group: Both sides of the formula live in the rational Chow ring of $Y$.
concepts.c:is-closed-immersion: The first factor of $f$ is a closed embedding.
concepts.c:normal-bundle: The normal bundle carries the Todd class correction for the embedding.

source.ref: A. Borel and J.-P. Serre, Le théorème de Riemann-Roch, Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France 86 (1958), 97-136
source.note: Borel and Serre's account of Grothendieck's proof by factorization into an embedding and a projection; W. Fulton, Intersection Theory, Chapter 15, gives a modern version.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) and $q$ a nondegenerate [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) over $K$. Then $q$ represents $0$ nontrivially over $K$ if and only if it does so over the [completion](c:completion) $K_v$ at every [place](c:place) $v$. Two nondegenerate quadratic forms over $K$ are equivalent over $K$ if and only if they are equivalent over every $K_v$.

hypotheses.text: The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field).
The [quadratic forms](c:quadratic-form) are nondegenerate.

conclusion: Isotropy and equivalence of nondegenerate [quadratic forms](c:quadratic-form) over $K$ hold exactly when they hold at every [place](c:place).

proofs.name: Induction on the rank
proofs.slogan: Prove the isotropy statement rank by rank with squares, norms, Hilbert symbols and approximation, then deduce equivalence by Witt cancellation.
proofs.scope: An outline: the global inputs of steps 1 to 3 rest on class field theory as in the cited works, and they are elementary over $\mathbb Q$. Only the converse directions need proof, because a global zero or a global equivalence is also local.

roles.why: The global inputs on squares, norms, Hilbert symbols and approximation hold for number fields.
Nondegenerate forms diagonalize with nonzero coefficients, and Witt cancellation applies to them.

steps.slogan: Settle rank 2 because a local square at every place is a global square.
steps.detail: Rank 1 forms are anisotropic everywhere, so start with $q \cong a\langle 1, -d\rangle$, which is isotropic exactly when $d$ is a square. If $d$ were not a square in $K$, the Chebotarev density theorem would give infinitely many places inert in $K(\sqrt d)$, where $d$ is not a local square.

steps.slogan: Settle rank 3 by writing isotropy as a norm condition from a quadratic extension.
steps.detail: Scale $q$ to $\langle 1, -b, -c\rangle$ with $b$ not a square; then $q$ is isotropic exactly when $c$ is a norm from $L = K(\sqrt b)$, and the same holds at each place. A local norm at every place is a global norm for the cyclic extension $L/K$ by the Hasse norm theorem.

steps.slogan: Settle rank 4 with a global element that has prescribed [Hilbert symbols](c:hilbert-symbol) at every place.
steps.detail: Write $q = \langle a_1, a_2\rangle \perp \langle -a_3, -a_4\rangle$ and choose local values $t_v$ represented by both halves. Hilbert reciprocity and the existence theorem for prescribed symbols give $t \in K^\times$ with the same symbols as the $t_v$, so $\langle a_1, a_2, -t\rangle$ and $\langle a_3, a_4, -t\rangle$ are isotropic everywhere, hence over $K$ by step 2.

steps.slogan: Settle rank at least 5 by induction with a value chosen through weak approximation.
steps.detail: Write $q = g \perp -h$ with $g$ of rank 2; outside a finite set $S$ of places, $h$ is a unit form of rank at least 3 at a non-dyadic place, hence isotropic. Weak approximation gives $t = g(x)$ near common local values $t_v$ for $v \in S$, so $\langle t\rangle \perp -h$ is isotropic everywhere and, by induction, $h$ represents $t$ over $K$.

steps.slogan: Deduce the equivalence statement by splitting off a common value and cancelling it.
steps.detail: With the isotropy statement of steps 1 to 4, if $q \cong q'$ everywhere and $q$ represents $a$, then $q' \perp \langle -a\rangle$ is isotropic everywhere, so $q'$ represents $a$ over $K$. Split $\langle a\rangle$ off both forms; Witt cancellation makes the complements equivalent at every place, and induction on the rank finishes.

concepts.c:number-field: The local-global inputs of the proof are theorems about number fields.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: Quadratic forms are the objects compared locally and globally.
concepts.c:completion: Local isotropy is tested over each completion $K_v$.
concepts.c:place: Each place gives a completion and a local Hilbert symbol.
concepts.c:hilbert-symbol: Hilbert symbols record local representability in the rank 4 step.

source.ref: O. T. O'Meara, Introduction to Quadratic Forms, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 117, Springer, 1963, Chapter VI; J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973, Chapter IV (the rational case)
source.note: The rank-by-rank structure follows Serre's proof over the rationals; over a number field the inputs for ranks 2 to 4 come from class field theory, as in O'Meara.

statement: Let $A$ be a closed prenex formula of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic) without equality, and let $\exists \bar x\, \varphi(\bar x)$ be its Herbrand form, the dual of [Skolemization](c:skolemization), with $\varphi$ quantifier-free. Then $A$ is [valid](c:validity) if and only if some finite disjunction $\varphi(\bar t_1) \vee \dots \vee \varphi(\bar t_k)$ of closed-term instances is a propositional [tautology](c:tautology).

hypotheses.text: The formula $A$ is a closed formula in prenex form.
The language of $A$ has no equality symbol, as a fragment of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic).

conclusion: Validity of $A$ is equivalent to a finite propositional [tautology](c:tautology) built from instances of $\varphi$.

proofs.name: Propositional compactness and a Herbrand model
proofs.slogan: Reduce to the Herbrand form, and if no disjunction of instances is a tautology, build a term model that falsifies it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; a constant symbol is added when the language has none, so closed terms exist. The direction from a tautology to validity is direct.

roles.why: The prenex form defines the Herbrand form and its quantifier-free matrix $\varphi$.
Without equality, relations on closed terms can follow any truth assignment.

steps.slogan: Show that $A$ is valid exactly when its Herbrand form is valid.
steps.detail:
The Herbrand form of $A$ is the negation of the Skolem form of $
eg A$. [Skolemization](c:skolemization) keeps satisfiability: a model of $
eg A$ interprets the new function symbols by chosen witnesses, and the Skolem form implies $
eg A$. So $
eg A$ has a model exactly when the negated Herbrand form has one.

steps.slogan: Check that a tautologous disjunction of instances makes the Herbrand form valid.
steps.detail: In every structure the tautology $\varphi(\bar t_1) \vee \dots \vee \varphi(\bar t_k)$ is true, so some $\varphi(\bar t_i)$ is true. Its terms witness $\exists \bar x\, \varphi$, so the Herbrand form is valid.

steps.slogan: Find one truth assignment that makes every negated instance true.
steps.detail: Suppose no finite disjunction is a tautology, and treat closed atomic formulas as propositional variables. Then every finite set of formulas $\neg\varphi(\bar t)$ is satisfiable, so compactness gives one assignment that makes all of them true.

steps.slogan: Build the Herbrand structure on closed terms from that truth assignment.
steps.detail: Let the domain be the set of closed terms, let function symbols act by forming terms, and let a relation hold on terms exactly when the assignment makes that atom true. With no equality to respect, this is a [structure](c:structure-model-theory) where every closed quantifier-free formula has the value of the assignment, so $\forall \bar x\, \neg\varphi$ holds and the Herbrand form fails.

steps.slogan: Combine the three parts to get the equivalence for $A$.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives one direction for the Herbrand form. Steps 3 and 4 show that the Herbrand form is not valid when no disjunction is a tautology, and step 1 transfers both directions to $A$.

concepts.c:first-order-logic: The theorem reduces first-order validity to propositional checks.
concepts.c:skolemization: Skolemization of $\neg A$ gives the Herbrand form of $A$.
concepts.c:validity: Validity of $A$ is the property that the theorem characterizes.
concepts.c:tautology: A tautologous disjunction is the finite certificate of validity.
concepts.c:structure-model-theory: The term structure is the countermodel built in step 4.

source.note: The standard proof by propositional compactness and Herbrand models, as in S. R. Buss, On Herbrand's theorem, in Logic and Computational Complexity, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 960, Springer, 1995.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonsingular complex [projective variety](c:projective-variety) and $E$ a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) on $X$. Then the [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) $\chi(X, E) = \sum_i (-1)^i \dim H^i(X, E)$ of its [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) equals $\int_X \mathrm{ch}(E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X)$, with the [Chern character](c:chern-character) $\mathrm{ch}$ and the [Todd class](c:todd-class) $\mathrm{td}$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a nonsingular complex [projective variety](c:projective-variety).
The bundle $E$ is a [holomorphic vector bundle](c:holomorphic-vector-bundle) on $X$.

proofs.name: Embedding into projective space
proofs.slogan: Embed the variety in projective space, check the formula there on line bundles, and transport it with the embedding case of Riemann-Roch.
proofs.scope: An outline; the embedding formula of step 4 rests on the cited work. Serre's GAGA makes analytic and algebraic cohomology agree on $X$, so the proof works algebraically.

roles.why: Projectivity gives the embedding into $\mathbb P^N$ and makes GAGA apply.
A vector bundle gives a coherent sheaf $i_*E$ with a Chern character.

steps.slogan: Embed $X$ in $\mathbb P^N$ and push $E$ forward to a [coherent sheaf](c:coherent-sheaf).
steps.detail: Projectivity gives a closed embedding $i\colon X \to \mathbb P^N$. The direct image $i_*E$ is coherent, $i_*$ is exact and $H^q(\mathbb P^N, i_*E) = H^q(X, E)$, so $\chi(X, E) = \chi(\mathbb P^N, i_*E)$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the formula on $\mathbb P^N$ to the line bundles $\mathcal O(k)$.
steps.detail: Both $\chi$ and $\int \mathrm{ch}(\cdot)\,\mathrm{td}(T_{\mathbb P^N})$ are additive on short exact sequences. Every coherent sheaf on $\mathbb P^N$ has a finite resolution by sums of line bundles $\mathcal O(k)$, by Serre's theorem and the syzygy theorem, so these classes suffice.

steps.slogan: Compute both sides for $\mathcal O(k)$ on [projective space](c:projective-space).
steps.detail: Here $\chi(\mathbb P^N, \mathcal O(k)) = \binom{N+k}{N}$. With $h$ the hyperplane class, the Euler sequence gives $\mathrm{td}(T_{\mathbb P^N}) = (h/(1 - e^{-h}))^{N+1}$, and the coefficient of $h^N$ in $e^{kh}(h/(1 - e^{-h}))^{N+1}$ is a residue that also equals $\binom{N+k}{N}$.

steps.slogan: Transport the formula from $\mathbb P^N$ to $X$ with Riemann-Roch for the embedding.
steps.detail: The cited work proves $\mathrm{ch}(i_*E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_{\mathbb P^N}) = i_*(\mathrm{ch}(E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X))$ for a closed embedding of smooth varieties. Its key input is the Koszul resolution along the normal bundle of $X$.

steps.slogan: Integrate over $\mathbb P^N$ to obtain $\chi(X, E) = \int_X \mathrm{ch}(E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X)$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 give $\chi(X, E) = \chi(\mathbb P^N, i_*E) = \int_{\mathbb P^N} \mathrm{ch}(i_*E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_{\mathbb P^N}) = \int_{\mathbb P^N} i_*(\mathrm{ch}(E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X))$. Pushforward keeps the degree of zero-cycles, so the last integral is $\int_X \mathrm{ch}(E)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X)$.

concepts.c:projective-variety: Projectivity lets the proof work inside $\mathbb P^N$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-vector-bundle: The bundle $E$ is the object whose cohomology the formula counts.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The alternating sum of cohomology dimensions is the left side.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The groups $H^i(X, E)$ define the Euler characteristic.
concepts.c:chern-character: The Chern character of $E$ enters the right side.
concepts.c:todd-class: The Todd class of $T_X$ is the correction factor in the integrand.
concepts.c:coherent-sheaf: The pushforward of $E$ is a coherent sheaf on $\mathbb P^N$.
concepts.c:projective-space: Line bundles on projective space give the explicit check.

source.ref: A. Borel and J.-P. Serre, Le théorème de Riemann-Roch, Bulletin de la Société Mathématique de France 86 (1958), 97-136
source.note: Grothendieck's proof as written by Borel and Serre; Hirzebruch's original cobordism proof is in F. Hirzebruch, Topological Methods in Algebraic Geometry, Springer, 1966.

statement: Let $M$ be a closed [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold). The analytic index $K^0(T^*M) \to \mathbb Z$, defined in [KK-theory](c:kk-theory) by the tangent groupoid, equals the topological index built from an embedding $M \subset \mathbb R^N$, the [Thom isomorphism](c:thom-isomorphism) and Bott periodicity. So the [Fredholm index](c:fredholm-index) of every [elliptic operator](c:elliptic-operator) on $M$ equals the topological index of its symbol class.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is a compact [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) without boundary.
The operator $D$ is an [elliptic](c:elliptic-operator) pseudodifferential operator on $M$ with symbol class $[\sigma_D] \in K^0(T^*M)$.

proofs.name: Connes' tangent groupoid
proofs.slogan: Realize the analytic index by the tangent groupoid deformation, then let the groupoid act on Euclidean space to identify it with the Thom and Bott maps.
proofs.scope: An outline of Connes' proof; steps 3 and 4 rest on the cited work. The record names a family of index theorems, and this is their K-theoretic form for closed manifolds.

roles.why: Compactness makes elliptic operators Fredholm and gives an embedding $M \subset \mathbb R^N$.
Ellipticity gives the symbol class in $K^0(T^*M)$ and the Fredholm property of $D$.

steps.slogan: Build the tangent groupoid that deforms $TM$ into the pair groupoid $M \times M$.
steps.detail: Let $G = TM \times \{0\} \cup M \times M \times (0, 1]$ with Connes' smooth structure. Its [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra) restricts at $t = 0$ to $C^*(TM) \cong C_0(T^*M)$ and at $t = 1$ to the compact operators $\mathcal K$ on $L^2(M)$.

steps.slogan: Define the analytic index as evaluation at $t = 1$ after inverting evaluation at $t = 0$.
steps.detail: The kernel of evaluation at $0$ is $C_0((0, 1]) \otimes \mathcal K$, which is contractible, so $(e_0)_*$ is an isomorphism in [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory). The map $\operatorname{ind}_a = (e_1)_* (e_0)_*^{-1}\colon K^0(T^*M) \to K_0(\mathcal K) = \mathbb Z$ sends $[\sigma_D]$ to the [Fredholm index](c:fredholm-index) of $D$, because $D$ and its symbol form one class on $G$.

steps.slogan: Let the tangent groupoid act on $\mathbb R^N$ through an embedding $M \subset \mathbb R^N$.
steps.detail: The map $h(x, y, t) = (x - y)/t$, $h(x, \xi, 0) = \xi$ is a groupoid homomorphism $G \to \mathbb R^N$. The Connes-[Thom isomorphism](c:thom-isomorphism) $K_*(A) \cong K_{*+N}(A \rtimes \mathbb R^N)$ is natural, so the crossed product deformation has the same index map.

steps.slogan: Replace the crossed products by functions on the orbit spaces of the free proper action.
steps.detail: The cited work shows that the action is free and proper, so each crossed product is Morita equivalent to functions on its orbit space. At $t = 0$ the orbit space is the normal bundle $\nu$ of $M$ in $\mathbb R^N$, at $t = 1$ it is $\mathbb R^N$, and the index map becomes extension by zero from a tubular neighborhood $\nu \subset \mathbb R^N$.

steps.slogan: Identify the resulting composite with the topological index.
steps.detail: The composite is the Thom isomorphism for $T^*M \subset T^*\mathbb R^N$, extension by zero from the tubular neighborhood, and the Bott isomorphism $K^0(\mathbb R^{2N}) \cong \mathbb Z$. This is the definition of $\operatorname{ind}_t$, so $\operatorname{ind}_a = \operatorname{ind}_t$ and $\operatorname{ind} D = \operatorname{ind}_t[\sigma_D]$.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The closed manifold carries the operators and embeds in $\mathbb R^N$.
concepts.c:kk-theory: KK-classes of the deformation define the analytic index map.
concepts.c:thom-isomorphism: Thom isomorphisms move the index between $T^*M$, $\nu$ and $\mathbb R^N$.
concepts.c:fredholm-index: The Fredholm index of $D$ is the analytic side of the theorem.
concepts.c:elliptic-operator: Elliptic operators have symbol classes and Fredholm indices.
concepts.c:c-star-algebra: The groupoid C*-algebra carries the deformation in K-theory.
concepts.c:topological-k-theory: Symbol classes and both index maps live in K-theory.

source.ref: A. Connes, Noncommutative Geometry, Academic Press, San Diego, 1994, Chapter II, Section 5
source.note: Connes' tangent groupoid proof of the K-theoretic index theorem of M. F. Atiyah and I. M. Singer, The index of elliptic operators I, Annals of Mathematics 87 (1968), 484-530.

statement: Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be [measurable spaces](c:measurable-space), $\mu_0$ a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $X_0$ and $\kappa_n$ a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) from $X_0 \times \dots \times X_n$ to $X_{n+1}$. Then exactly one probability measure $P$ on $\prod_n X_n$ has image $\mu_0 \otimes \kappa_0 \otimes \dots \otimes \kappa_{n-1}$ on $X_0 \times \dots \times X_n$ for every $n$. Constant kernels give the infinite [product measure](c:product-measure).

hypotheses.text: Each $X_n$ is a [measurable space](c:measurable-space), with no topological assumption.
The measure $\mu_0$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $X_0$.
Each $\kappa_n$ is a [Markov kernel](c:markov-kernel) from $X_0 \times \dots \times X_n$ to $X_{n+1}$.

conclusion: Exactly one probability measure on the trajectory space $\prod_n X_n$ has the given finite-dimensional marginals.

formal.difference: The declaration is a kernel $\mathrm{traj}\,\kappa\,a$ from the first $a + 1$ coordinates to $\prod_n X_n$, with marginals given by traj_map_frestrictLe and uniqueness by eq_traj. The measure with initial law $\mu_0$ is trajMeasure μ₀ κ, the composition of traj κ 0 with $\mu_0$.

proofs.name: Content on cylinder sets
proofs.slogan: Define the measure on cylinder sets, prove continuity at the empty set by choosing a point coordinate by coordinate, and extend by Carathéodory.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for arbitrary measurable spaces. The coordinate-by-coordinate choice of step 3 replaces the compactness that the Kolmogorov extension theorem needs.

roles.why: Cylinders and the choice of step 3 use only measurability, so no topology is needed.
The initial law $\mu_0$ starts the marginals $P_n$.
Total mass one gives consistency, and the kernels give the conditional probabilities of step 3.

steps.slogan: Form the measures $P_n = \mu_0 \otimes \kappa_0 \otimes \dots \otimes \kappa_{n-1}$ and check their consistency.
steps.detail: Each $P_n$ is a probability measure on $X_0 \times \dots \times X_n$. Integrating out the last coordinate of $P_{n+1}$ gives $P_n$, because $\kappa_n(x, X_{n+1}) = 1$ for every $x$.

steps.slogan: Define an additive [content](c:add-content) on measurable cylinder sets from the measures $P_n$.
steps.detail: A measurable cylinder is $C = S \times \prod_{i > n} X_i$ with $S$ measurable in $X_0 \times \dots \times X_n$; set $P(C) = P_n(S)$. Consistency makes this independent of the representation, and $P$ is finitely additive on the ring of cylinders.

steps.slogan: Show that the content tends to zero along decreasing cylinders with empty intersection.
steps.detail: Suppose cylinders $A_k$ decrease, $\bigcap_k A_k = \emptyset$ and $P(A_k) \ge \varepsilon > 0$. The conditional probabilities of $A_k$ given $x_0, \dots, x_n$ decrease in $k$, so monotone convergence lets one choose $x_0, x_1, \dots$ in turn with all these limits at least $\varepsilon$. Then the sequence $(x_n)$ lies in every $A_k$, which is a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Extend the content to a measure on the product [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) by Carathéodory's theorem.
steps.detail: A finitely additive content that is continuous at $\emptyset$ is countably additive on the ring of cylinders. Carathéodory's theorem extends it to a measure on the generated product sigma-algebra, with $P(\prod_n X_n) = P_0(X_0) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Prove uniqueness on the π-system of cylinders with Dynkin's theorem.
steps.detail: Two probability measures with the given marginals agree on all measurable cylinders. Cylinders are closed under finite intersections and generate the product sigma-algebra, so Dynkin's π-λ theorem makes the measures equal; with step 4 this gives existence and uniqueness.

concepts.c:measurable-space: The factors are bare measurable spaces, so cylinders are the only tool.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The initial law and the result are probability measures.
concepts.c:markov-kernel: The kernels give the marginals and the conditional probabilities.
concepts.c:product-measure: With constant kernels the construction yields the infinite product measure.
concepts.c:add-content: The finitely additive content on cylinders is the object extended.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cylinders.

statement: Let $X$ be a compact triangulable space and $f\colon X \to X$ a continuous map with [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) $L(f) = \sum_k (-1)^k \operatorname{tr}\bigl(f_*\colon H_k(X;\mathbb Q) \to H_k(X;\mathbb Q)\bigr)$ in rational [homology](c:homology). If $L(f) \neq 0$, then $f$ has a [fixed point](c:fixed-point).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is compact and homeomorphic to a finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex).
The map $f\colon X \to X$ is continuous.
The [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) $L(f)$ is not zero.

proofs.name: Simplicial approximation and the Hopf trace formula
proofs.slogan: Assume no fixed point, approximate $f$ by a simplicial map that moves every simplex off itself, and compute a zero alternating trace.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, by contradiction. Rational coefficients make the chain and homology groups finite-dimensional vector spaces with traces.

roles.why: The triangulation gives simplicial chains, subdivisions and a compact metric.
Continuity makes the displacement function continuous and allows simplicial approximation.
A nonzero Lefschetz number contradicts the zero trace.

steps.slogan: Find $\varepsilon > 0$ with $d(x, f(x)) \ge \varepsilon$ for all $x$ when $f$ has no fixed point.
steps.detail: Give $X = |K|$ the metric of the finite simplicial complex $K$. The continuous function $x \mapsto d(x, f(x))$ is positive on the [compact](c:compact-space) space $X$, so it has a positive minimum $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Subdivide and take a simplicial approximation $g$ that moves every simplex off itself.
steps.detail: Subdivide $K$ so that every simplex has diameter less than $\varepsilon/3$, and take a further subdivision $L$ and a simplicial approximation $g\colon L \to K$ of $f$, homotopic to $f$ with $d(g(x), f(x)) < \varepsilon/3$. Then $d(g(x), x) > 2\varepsilon/3$, so $g(\sigma) \cap \sigma = \emptyset$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [chain map](c:chain-map) $g_\# \circ \mathrm{sd}$ has trace zero in every degree.
steps.detail: The subdivision chain map sends a simplex $\sigma$ of $K$ to a sum of simplices of $L$ inside $\sigma$, and $g$ sends these into simplices disjoint from $\sigma$. So the coefficient of $\sigma$ in $g_\# \mathrm{sd}(\sigma)$ is zero, and every trace on $C_k(K; \mathbb Q)$ vanishes.

steps.slogan: Pass the alternating trace from chains to homology with the Hopf trace formula.
steps.detail: Trace is additive on the exact sequences $0 \to Z_k \to C_k \to B_{k-1} \to 0$ and $0 \to B_k \to Z_k \to H_k \to 0$, so the alternating trace on chains equals the alternating trace on [homology](c:homology). The map induced by $g_\# \mathrm{sd}$ is $f_*$, because $\mathrm{sd}$ induces the identity and $g$ is homotopic to $f$.

steps.slogan: Conclude $L(f) = 0$, which contradicts the hypothesis, so $f$ has a fixed point.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $L(f) = \sum_k (-1)^k \operatorname{tr}(g_\# \mathrm{sd})_k = 0$. This contradicts $L(f) \neq 0$, so the assumption of step 1 fails and some $x$ has $f(x) = x$.

concepts.c:lefschetz-number: The Lefschetz number is the alternating trace computed in two ways.
concepts.c:homology: Rational homology carries the traces that define $L(f)$.
concepts.c:fixed-point: A fixed point is what the contradiction produces.
concepts.c:simplicial-complex: The triangulation supplies simplicial chains and small simplices.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives a positive minimum displacement $\varepsilon$.
concepts.c:chain-map: The chain map $g_\# \mathrm{sd}$ has zero trace on chains.

source.note: The proof of A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (2002), Theorem 2C.3.

statement: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb C$ be open and $\mathcal F$ a family of [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$ that is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $U$. Then $\mathcal F$ is a [normal family](c:normal-family): every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a subsequence that converges [locally uniformly](c:locally-uniform-convergence) on $U$ to a holomorphic function.

hypotheses.text: The set $U \subseteq \mathbb C$ is open.
Every member of $\mathcal F$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$.
For each compact $K \subseteq U$ some $M_K$ bounds $|f|$ on $K$ for all $f \in \mathcal F$.

conclusion: Every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a subsequence that converges uniformly on compact subsets of $U$.

proofs.name: Cauchy estimates and Arzelà-Ascoli
proofs.slogan: Bound derivatives by Cauchy's estimate to get equicontinuity, apply Arzelà-Ascoli on compact sets, and diagonalize over an exhaustion.
proofs.scope: The first Montel theorem; the theorem on families that omit two values is a separate result. An empty $U$ or a finite family needs no argument.

roles.why: Openness gives closed disks around each point and an exhaustion by compact sets.
Holomorphy gives Cauchy's estimate and a holomorphic limit.
Local bounds give the constant $M$ and pointwise boundedness.

steps.slogan: Bound the derivatives of the whole family on each small disk by Cauchy's estimate.
steps.detail: If the closed disk $\overline D(a, 2r)$ lies in $U$ and $|f| \le M$ on it for all $f \in \mathcal F$, Cauchy's estimate on circles of radius $r$ gives $|f'(z)| \le M/r$ for every $z \in D(a, r)$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that the family is [equicontinuous](c:equicontinuity) on each compact subset of $U$.
steps.detail: On $D(a, r)$ every $f \in \mathcal F$ is Lipschitz with constant $M/r$, so $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous at every point. A finite cover of a compact set by such disks makes this uniform on the compact set.

steps.slogan: Extract on each compact set a uniformly convergent subsequence with the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem.
steps.detail: On a compact $K \subseteq U$ the family is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. The Arzelà-Ascoli theorem then gives, from any sequence, a subsequence that converges uniformly on $K$.

steps.slogan: Diagonalize over an exhaustion of $U$ by compact sets.
steps.detail: Let $K_m = \{z \in U : |z| \le m,\ \operatorname{dist}(z, \mathbb C \setminus U) \ge 1/m\}$, so every compact subset of $U$ lies in some $K_m$. Take nested subsequences that converge on $K_1, K_2, \dots$; the diagonal subsequence converges uniformly on every $K_m$.

steps.slogan: Show that the locally uniform limit is holomorphic.
steps.detail: A [locally uniform](c:locally-uniform-convergence) limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic, because Morera's criterion passes to the limit. So the diagonal subsequence converges to a holomorphic function, and $\mathcal F$ is normal.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives derivative bounds and a holomorphic limit.
concepts.c:normal-family: Normality is the compactness property that the theorem proves.
concepts.c:locally-uniform-convergence: The subsequence converges uniformly on every compact subset.
concepts.c:equicontinuity: Equicontinuity is the hypothesis that Arzelà-Ascoli needs.

statement: Consider $n \ge 2$ risky assets with mean return vector $\mu$, not a multiple of $\mathbf 1 = (1, \dots, 1)$, and positive definite [covariance matrix](c:covariance-matrix) $\Sigma$, with short sales allowed. For each target mean $m$ the minimum-variance portfolio $w(m)$ is unique and affine in $m$. So any two distinct frontier portfolios generate every portfolio on the [efficient frontier](c:efficient-frontier).

hypotheses.text: The mean vector $\mu \in \mathbb R^n$ is not a multiple of $\mathbf 1$.
The [covariance matrix](c:covariance-matrix) $\Sigma$ is [positive definite](c:positive-definite-matrix).
A portfolio is any $w \in \mathbb R^n$ with $\mathbf 1^\top w = 1$, so short sales are allowed.

conclusion: Frontier portfolios satisfy $w(m) = g + m h$ for fixed vectors $g$ and $h$, and any two distinct frontier portfolios generate all of them.

proofs.name: Lagrange multipliers
proofs.slogan: Solve the [mean-variance](c:mean-variance-optimization) problem with Lagrange multipliers and observe that the solution is affine in the target mean.
proofs.scope: Every target mean $m \in \mathbb R$. Efficient portfolios are the frontier portfolios with $m \ge A/C$ in the notation of step 3.

roles.why: Independence of $\mu$ and $\mathbf 1$ makes the constraints consistent and gives $D > 0$.
Positive definiteness gives a unique minimizer and the inner product of step 3.
Without sign constraints the only constraints are two equations, so the Lagrange condition holds.

steps.slogan: Show that the constrained variance problem has exactly one minimizer for each target mean.
steps.detail: The constraints $\mathbf 1^\top w = 1$ and $\mu^\top w = m$ define a nonempty affine subspace, because $\mu$ and $\mathbf 1$ are independent. The variance $w^\top \Sigma w$ is strictly convex and coercive there because $\Sigma$ is positive definite, so it has a unique minimizer $w(m)$.

steps.slogan: Write the [Lagrange multiplier](c:lagrange-multiplier) condition $\Sigma w = \lambda \mu + \gamma \mathbf 1$ at the minimizer.
steps.detail: At the minimizer the gradient $2\Sigma w$ lies in the span of the constraint gradients $\mu$ and $\mathbf 1$. So $w(m) = \Sigma^{-1}(\lambda\mu + \gamma\mathbf 1)$ for some real numbers $\lambda$ and $\gamma$.

steps.slogan: Solve the $2 \times 2$ system for $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ as affine functions of $m$.
steps.detail: With $A = \mathbf 1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu$, $B = \mu^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu$ and $C = \mathbf 1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1$, the constraints read $B\lambda + A\gamma = m$ and $A\lambda + C\gamma = 1$. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for $\langle u, v\rangle = u^\top\Sigma^{-1}v$ gives $D = BC - A^2 > 0$, so $\lambda = (Cm - A)/D$ and $\gamma = (B - Am)/D$.

steps.slogan: Substitute to get $w(m) = g + m h$ with fixed vectors $g$ and $h$.
steps.detail: Substitution gives $g = (B\,\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1 - A\,\Sigma^{-1}\mu)/D$ and $h = (C\,\Sigma^{-1}\mu - A\,\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf 1)/D$. Neither vector depends on $m$.

steps.slogan: Write every frontier portfolio as a combination of two distinct frontier portfolios.
steps.detail: For $m_1 \ne m_2$ and $\alpha = (m - m_2)/(m_1 - m_2)$, affinity gives $w(m) = \alpha\, w(m_1) + (1 - \alpha)\, w(m_2)$. So two funds generate the whole frontier, and in particular every efficient portfolio.

concepts.c:covariance-matrix: The covariance matrix defines the variance that the portfolio minimizes.
concepts.c:positive-definite-matrix: Positive definiteness gives strict convexity and an inner product.
concepts.c:efficient-frontier: The efficient frontier is the set that two funds generate.
concepts.c:mean-variance-optimization: The frontier portfolios solve the mean-variance problem.
concepts.c:lagrange-multiplier: The multipliers $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ carry the dependence on $m$.

source.note: The frontier computation of R. C. Merton, An analytic derivation of the efficient portfolio frontier, Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 7 (1972), 1851-1872.

statement: Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be variables over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, with [elementary symmetric polynomials](c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial) $e_j$ and [power sums](c:power-sum) $p_j = x_1^j + \dots + x_n^j$. Then $k\,e_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (-1)^{i-1} e_{k-i}\, p_i$ in the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ for every $k \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficient ring $R$ is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring).
There are finitely many variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$.
The index $k$ is a positive integer.

formal.difference: The declaration writes the sum over antidiagonal pairs $(a, b)$ with $a + b = k$ and $a < k$, with a global sign $(-1)^{k+1}$. It also covers the trivial case $k = 0$.

proofs.name: Zeilberger's sign-reversing involution
proofs.slogan: Write both sides as weights of pairs $(A, j)$ and cancel the weights with a sign-reversing [involution](c:involution).
proofs.scope: Every $k \ge 1$ and every $n$, including $k > n$ where $e_k = 0$. The proof works directly in $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$.

roles.why: Commutativity makes $x^A x_j^{k - |A|}$ a well-defined monomial, so weights cancel.
Finitely many variables make the set of pairs finite.
For $k \ge 1$ the pairs with $|A| = k$ give the term $k\,e_k$.

steps.slogan: Define the pairs $(A, j)$ and their signed weights $(-1)^{|A|} x^A x_j^{k - |A|}$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal P$ be the finite set of pairs with $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, n\}$, $|A| \le k$, $j \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, and $j \in A$ when $|A| = k$. Give $(A, j)$ the weight $w(A, j) = (-1)^{|A|}\, x^A x_j^{k - |A|}$, where $x^A = \prod_{a \in A} x_a$.

steps.slogan: Toggle $j$ in $A$ to get an involution of the pairs that reverses each weight.
steps.detail: Let $\tau(A, j) = (A \setminus \{j\}, j)$ if $j \in A$ and $\tau(A, j) = (A \cup \{j\}, j)$ otherwise. This map sends $\mathcal P$ to $\mathcal P$, has no fixed point, and satisfies $w(\tau(t)) = -w(t)$, because the monomial stays the same and $|A|$ changes by one. So $\sum_{t \in \mathcal P} w(t) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Sum the weights with $|A| = k$ to get $(-1)^k k\, e_k$.
steps.detail: Here $j \in A$ and the weight is $(-1)^k x^A$. Each $k$-set $A$ appears with its $k$ choices of $j$, so these weights sum to $(-1)^k k\, e_k$.

steps.slogan: Sum the weights with $|A| = a < k$ to get $(-1)^a e_a\, p_{k-a}$.
steps.detail: Here $j$ is arbitrary, so the sum over $A$ and $j$ factors as $(-1)^a \bigl(\sum_{|A| = a} x^A\bigr)\bigl(\sum_j x_j^{k-a}\bigr) = (-1)^a e_a\, p_{k-a}$.

steps.slogan: Add the parts and solve for $k\, e_k$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 to 4 give $(-1)^k k\, e_k + \sum_{a=0}^{k-1} (-1)^a e_a\, p_{k-a} = 0$. Multiplying by $(-1)^{k+1}$ and putting $i = k - a$ gives $k\, e_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (-1)^{i-1} e_{k-i}\, p_i$.

concepts.c:commutative-ring: Commutativity lets equal monomials from different terms combine.
concepts.c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial: The polynomials $e_j$ form one side of the identity.
concepts.c:power-sum: The power sums $p_i$ form the other side of the identity.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The identity holds in $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ itself.
concepts.c:involution: The sign-reversing involution cancels all weights in pairs.

proofs.name: Logarithmic derivative
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the [generating function](c:generating-function) $E(t) = \prod_i (1 + x_i t)$ and compare coefficients in $E' = E \cdot P$.
proofs.scope: Every $k \ge 1$. The computation takes place in [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) in $t$ over $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$.

roles.why: Commutativity makes the coefficients of $E(t)$ the polynomials $e_k$.
Finitely many factors make $E(t)$ a polynomial and the product rule a finite sum.
The coefficient of $t^{k-1}$ in $E'(t)$ exists only for $k \ge 1$.

steps.slogan: Expand $E(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1 + x_i t)$ as $\sum_k e_k t^k$.
steps.detail: Choosing $x_i t$ from the factors indexed by a $k$-set $A$ and $1$ from the others gives $x^A t^k$. Summing over all $A$ gives $E(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} e_k t^k$ in $R[x_1, \dots, x_n][t]$.

steps.slogan: Compute $E'(t) = E(t) \sum_{m \ge 0} (-1)^m p_{m+1} t^m$ by the product rule.
steps.detail: The product rule gives $E'(t) = \sum_i x_i \prod_{j \ne i} (1 + x_j t)$. In [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) each $1 + x_i t$ has the inverse $\sum_m (-x_i t)^m$, so $E'(t) = E(t) \sum_i x_i (1 + x_i t)^{-1} = E(t) \sum_{m \ge 0} (-1)^m p_{m+1} t^m$.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $t^{k-1}$ on both sides.
steps.detail: The coefficient of $t^{k-1}$ in $E'(t)$ is $k\, e_k$. On the right it is $\sum_{m=0}^{k-1} (-1)^m p_{m+1} e_{k-1-m}$, which is $\sum_{i=1}^{k} (-1)^{i-1} e_{k-i}\, p_i$ with $i = m + 1$.

concepts.c:commutative-ring: Commutativity lets equal monomials from different terms combine.
concepts.c:elementary-symmetric-polynomial: The polynomials $e_j$ form one side of the identity.
concepts.c:power-sum: The power sums $p_i$ form the other side of the identity.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The identity holds in $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ itself.
concepts.c:generating-function: The generating function $E(t)$ packages all $e_k$ at once.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: Inverting $1 + x_i t$ needs formal power series in $t$.

statement: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb C$ be a nonempty connected [open set](c:open-set) and $f\colon U \to \mathbb C$ a non-constant [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function). Then $f$ is an [open map](c:open-map): $f(V)$ is open for every open $V \subseteq U$.

hypotheses.text: The set $U \subseteq \mathbb C$ is open and [connected](c:connected-space).
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$.
The function $f$ is not constant on $U$.

conclusion: Every open $V \subseteq U$ has an open image $f(V)$.

formal.difference: The declaration takes $g\colon E \to \mathbb C$ on any complex normed space, analytic on a neighborhood of a preconnected set $U$. It concludes that $g$ is constant on $U$ or maps every open subset of $U$ to an open set.

proofs.name: Isolated zeros and the maximum modulus principle
proofs.slogan: Show that $f$ is nowhere locally constant, bound $|f - f(z_0)|$ below on a small circle, and reach each nearby value with the maximum modulus principle.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the identity theorem decides between the locally constant case and the other case. An empty $V$ has the open image $\emptyset$.

roles.why: Connectedness lets the identity theorem spread local constancy to all of $U$.
Holomorphy gives isolated zeros and the maximum modulus principle.
Non-constancy rules out local constancy at every point.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ is constant on no neighborhood of any point of $U$.
steps.detail: If $f = f(z_0)$ near some $z_0$, the identity theorem on the [connected](c:connected-space) set $U$ makes $f$ constant on $U$. This contradicts the hypothesis, so $f$ is nowhere locally constant.

steps.slogan: Choose a circle around $z_0$ on which $|f - f(z_0)|$ has a positive minimum $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Fix $z_0 \in V$. By step 1 the zeros of $f - f(z_0)$ are isolated, so some $r > 0$ has $\overline D(z_0, r) \subseteq V$ and $f \ne f(z_0)$ on the circle $|z - z_0| = r$. The circle is compact, so $\varepsilon = \min |f - f(z_0)| > 0$ there.

steps.slogan: Show that $|f - w|$ has its minimum inside the disk when $|w - f(z_0)| < \varepsilon/2$.
steps.detail: The continuous function $|f - w|$ has a minimum on the compact closed disk. On the circle $|f - w| \ge \varepsilon - \varepsilon/2 > |f(z_0) - w|$, so the minimum lies in the open disk.

steps.slogan: Force a zero of $f - w$ with the maximum modulus principle for $1/(f - w)$.
steps.detail: If $f - w$ had no zero in the disk, $1/(f - w)$ would be holomorphic there with an interior maximum of its modulus. The maximum modulus principle would make it constant near that point, against step 1. So $f(z) = w$ for some $z$ in the disk.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $f(V)$ contains a disk around each of its points.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $D(f(z_0), \varepsilon/2) \subseteq f(\overline D(z_0, r)) \subseteq f(V)$. Since $z_0 \in V$ was arbitrary, $f(V)$ is open.

concepts.c:open-set: The domain and the images of open subsets are open sets.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives isolated zeros and the local tools of the proof.
concepts.c:open-map: Openness of $f$ is the conclusion that the proof establishes.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness lets the identity theorem exclude local constancy.

proofs.name: Counting zeros with Rouché's theorem
proofs.slogan: Count the zeros of $f - w$ in a small disk with Rouché's theorem and compare them with the zeros of $f - f(z_0)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; step 1 uses the identity theorem as the first proof does. An empty $V$ has the open image $\emptyset$.

roles.why: Connectedness makes the zeros of $f - f(z_0)$ isolated through the identity theorem.
Holomorphy makes Rouché's theorem apply on the circle.
Non-constancy excludes $f - f(z_0) \equiv 0$ near $z_0$.

steps.slogan: Isolate the zero $z_0$ of $f - f(z_0)$ inside a small closed disk in $V$.
steps.detail: By the identity theorem on the [connected](c:connected-space) $U$, the non-constant function $f - f(z_0)$ has isolated zeros. So some $r > 0$ has $\overline D(z_0, r) \subseteq V$ and $|f - f(z_0)| \ge \delta > 0$ on the circle $|z - z_0| = r$.

steps.slogan: Compare $f - w$ with $f - f(z_0)$ on the circle by Rouché's theorem.
steps.detail: For $|w - f(z_0)| < \delta$, on the circle $|(f - w) - (f - f(z_0))| = |w - f(z_0)| < \delta \le |f - f(z_0)|$. Rouché's theorem gives $f - w$ as many zeros in the disk as $f - f(z_0)$, which has at least the zero $z_0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the disk $D(f(z_0), \delta)$ lies in $f(V)$.
steps.detail: Step 2 shows that every $w$ with $|w - f(z_0)| < \delta$ is a value of $f$ on $D(z_0, r) \subseteq V$. So $f(V)$ is a neighborhood of each of its points and is open.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives isolated zeros and the local tools of the proof.
concepts.c:open-map: Openness of $f$ is the conclusion that the proof establishes.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness lets the identity theorem exclude local constancy.

statement: Let $(M, g)$ be a connected, time-oriented [globally hyperbolic spacetime](c:globally-hyperbolic-spacetime) of dimension $n \ge 3$ with a non-compact [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface). If $\operatorname{Ric}(k, k) \ge 0$ for every null vector $k$ (the null [energy condition](c:energy-condition)) and $M$ contains a closed [trapped surface](c:trapped-surface), then $M$ is null [geodesically incomplete](c:geodesic-incompleteness).

hypotheses.text: The spacetime $(M, g)$ is connected, time-oriented and [globally hyperbolic](c:globally-hyperbolic-spacetime), of dimension $n \ge 3$.
Its [Cauchy surface](c:cauchy-surface) $\Sigma$ is non-compact.
The null [energy condition](c:energy-condition) $\operatorname{Ric}(k, k) \ge 0$ holds for every null vector $k$.
$M$ contains a closed [trapped surface](c:trapped-surface) $T$, a compact spacelike submanifold of codimension 2 on which both future null expansions are negative.

conclusion: Some null geodesic of $M$ is inextendible with finite affine length, so $M$ is [geodesically incomplete](c:geodesic-incompleteness).

proofs.name: Compact achronal boundary
proofs.slogan: Assume null completeness, show that the boundary of the future of the trapped surface is compact, and project it onto the non-compact Cauchy surface.
proofs.scope: An outline of Penrose's proof by contradiction; the causal-structure facts of steps 2 and 3 rest on the cited works.

roles.why: Global hyperbolicity makes $J^+(T)$ closed and gives the projection to $\Sigma$.
A non-compact $\Sigma$ cannot be the image of a compact set.
The energy condition drives the expansion to $-\infty$ in the Raychaudhuri equation.
Negative initial expansions on the compact $T$ give a uniform focusing bound.

steps.slogan: Find a [focal point](c:focal-point) on every null normal geodesic within a fixed parameter.
steps.detail: Assume that all null geodesics are complete. Along a future null normal geodesic of $T$ the Raychaudhuri equation and the energy condition give $d\theta/ds \le -\theta^2/(n - 2)$, so $\theta$ starting at $\theta_0 \le -c < 0$ reaches $-\infty$ by $s = (n - 2)/c$, which is a focal point.

steps.slogan: Show that the boundary of the causal future $J^+(T)$ is compact.
steps.detail: Global hyperbolicity makes $J^+(T)$ closed, and each point of $\partial J^+(T)$ lies on a null normal geodesic from $T$ before its first focal point, since beyond it the geodesic enters the timelike future. So $\partial J^+(T)$ is a closed part of the exponential image of the compact set $\{(p, k, s) : p \in T,\ s \le (n - 2)/c\}$, hence compact.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial J^+(T)$ is a closed achronal topological hypersurface without boundary.
steps.detail: The cited works show that the boundary of a future set is an achronal embedded $C^0$ hypersurface without boundary. With step 2 it is a compact topological $(n - 1)$-manifold.

steps.slogan: Push the boundary along a timelike field onto the Cauchy surface and reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: Global hyperbolicity gives a timelike vector field whose integral curves meet $\Sigma$ once and the achronal boundary at most once, so they define a continuous injection $\partial J^+(T) \to \Sigma$. By invariance of domain its image is open, and it is compact, so it is all of the connected $\Sigma$; then $\Sigma$ is compact, a contradiction, so some null geodesic is incomplete.

concepts.c:globally-hyperbolic-spacetime: Global hyperbolicity controls causal futures and gives the Cauchy surface.
concepts.c:cauchy-surface: The non-compact Cauchy surface receives the compact boundary.
concepts.c:energy-condition: The null energy condition makes null geodesics focus.
concepts.c:trapped-surface: The trapped surface starts the focusing with negative expansion.
concepts.c:geodesic-incompleteness: Incompleteness is the conclusion reached by contradiction.
concepts.c:focal-point: Focal points cut the null generators of the boundary short.

statement: Let $M$ be a compact [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) without boundary and $v$ a smooth [vector field](c:vector-field) on $M$ with only isolated zeros. Then the sum of the [indices](c:index-of-a-zero) of $v$ at its zeros equals the [Euler characteristic](c:euler-characteristic) $\chi(M)$.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is a compact [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) without boundary.
The smooth [vector field](c:vector-field) $v$ has only isolated zeros.

proofs.name: Gauss map and a Morse function
proofs.slogan: Show that the index sum equals the degree of a Gauss map, so it does not depend on $v$, then compute it for a gradient field.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the index is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of $v/|v|$ on a small sphere around a zero in a chart. A field without zeros gives the empty sum $0$.

roles.why: Compactness gives finitely many zeros, a tubular neighborhood and a finite cell structure.
Isolated zeros have well-defined local indices.

steps.slogan: Show that the zeros are finite in number, so the index sum is defined.
steps.detail: The zero set of $v$ is closed in the compact $M$, and each zero is isolated. A compact discrete set is finite, so the sum of the local indices is a finite sum.

steps.slogan: Equate the index sum with the degree of the Gauss map of a tubular neighborhood.
steps.detail: Embed $M$ in $\mathbb R^k$ and let $N$ be a closed $\varepsilon$-neighborhood with closest-point retraction $r$. The field $w(x) = (x - r(x)) + v(r(x))$ points outward on $\partial N$ and has the zeros of $v$ with the same indices, so the index sum equals the degree of the Gauss map $\partial N \to S^{k-1}$, which does not depend on $v$.

steps.slogan: Choose a [Morse function](c:morse-function) $f$ and take its gradient as a test field.
steps.detail: Morse functions exist on $M$: Sard's theorem makes almost every linear height function on $M \subset \mathbb R^k$ a Morse function. With a Riemannian metric, $\nabla f$ vanishes exactly at the critical points of $f$, which are nondegenerate and isolated.

steps.slogan: Compute the index of $\nabla f$ at a critical point of Morse index $\lambda$ as $(-1)^\lambda$.
steps.detail: The Morse lemma gives coordinates with $f = f(p) - x_1^2 - \dots - x_\lambda^2 + x_{\lambda+1}^2 + \dots + x_m^2$. There $\nabla f$ deforms, without zeros on a small sphere, to a linear field with $\lambda$ negative eigenvalues, whose index is the sign of its determinant, $(-1)^\lambda$.

steps.slogan: Count cells to get $\chi(M) = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda c_\lambda$.
steps.detail: Morse theory gives $M$ the homotopy type of a finite CW complex with one $\lambda$-cell for each critical point of index $\lambda$. The Euler characteristic of a finite CW complex is the alternating count of its cells.

steps.slogan: Combine the steps to get the index sum $\chi(M)$ for every field $v$.
steps.detail: By step 2 the index sum of $v$ equals the index sum of $\nabla f$. Steps 4 and 5 give $\sum_p (-1)^{\lambda(p)} = \sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda c_\lambda = \chi(M)$.

concepts.c:vector-field: The vector field supplies the zeros and their indices.
concepts.c:index-of-a-zero: Local indices are the terms of the sum that the theorem computes.
concepts.c:euler-characteristic: The Euler characteristic is the value of the index sum.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-map: Indices and the Gauss map invariant are degrees of maps to spheres.
concepts.c:morse-function: A Morse function gives a test field with computable indices.

source.note: J. Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint (1965), Section 6, with the cell count of J. Milnor, Morse Theory (1963), Theorem 3.5.

proofs.name: Lefschetz number of the flow
proofs.slogan: Compute the [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) of the short-time backward flow of $v$ by its fixed points and by homotopy to the identity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; a smooth compact manifold is triangulable, so the Lefschetz-Hopf theorem applies. A field without zeros gives the empty sum $0$.

roles.why: Compactness makes the flow global, the Lipschitz bound uniform and the Lefschetz number defined.
Isolated zeros are isolated fixed points with defined indices.

steps.slogan: Identify the fixed points of the backward [flow](c:flow-of-a-vector-field) $\phi_{-t}$ with the zeros of $v$.
steps.detail: Compactness makes the flow $\phi_t$ of $v$ global. A nonconstant periodic orbit has period at least $2\pi/L$ for a Lipschitz constant $L$ of $v$ (Yorke's bound), so for $0 < t < 2\pi/L$ the fixed points of $\phi_{-t}$ are exactly the zeros of $v$.

steps.slogan: Match the fixed-point index of $\phi_{-t}$ at each zero with the index of $v$.
steps.detail: In a chart, $x - \phi_{-t}(x) = \int_0^t v(\phi_{-s}(x))\,ds$ differs from $t\,v(x)$ by at most $L t^2 \max|v|$. For small $t$ this is less than $t|v|$ on a small sphere around the zero, so the two maps have the same [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) there, and the fixed-point index equals $\operatorname{ind}_p(v)$.

steps.slogan: Sum the local indices with the Lefschetz-Hopf theorem.
steps.detail: The Lefschetz-Hopf theorem states that the Lefschetz number of a map with finitely many fixed points is the sum of their indices. With steps 1 and 2 this gives $L(\phi_{-t}) = \sum_p \operatorname{ind}_p(v)$.

steps.slogan: Deform $\phi_{-t}$ to the identity to get $L(\phi_{-t}) = \chi(M)$.
steps.detail: The maps $\phi_{-s}$ for $0 \le s \le t$ form a homotopy from the identity to $\phi_{-t}$, so both have the same Lefschetz number. The identity has $L = \sum_k (-1)^k \dim H_k(M; \mathbb Q) = \chi(M)$, and step 3 finishes the proof.

statement: Let $T$ be a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ and $|T| = (T^*T)^{1/2}$ its [positive square root](c:positive-square-root). Then $T = U|T|$ for a [partial isometry](c:partial-isometry) $U$ with $\ker U = \ker T$. A factorization $T = VP$ with $P \ge 0$ and $V$ a partial isometry with $\ker V = \ker P$ is unique.

hypotheses.text: The space $H$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
The operator $T\colon H \to H$ is a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator).

conclusion: $T = U|T|$ with $U$ a [partial isometry](c:partial-isometry) and $\ker U = \ker T$, and $U$ and $|T|$ are the only such factors.

proofs.name: Isometry on the range
proofs.slogan: Show that $|T|x \mapsto Tx$ is a well-defined isometry, extend it by continuity and by zero, and get uniqueness from the square root.
proofs.scope: Every bounded $T$ in any dimension. $T = 0$ gives $U = 0$, and an invertible $T$ gives a unitary $U$.

roles.why: Completeness and orthogonal complements allow the extension and the zero part.
Boundedness makes $T^*T$ a bounded positive operator with a square root.

steps.slogan: Take the positive square root $|T|$ of the [positive operator](c:positive-operator) $T^*T$.
steps.detail: Since $\langle T^*Tx, x\rangle = \|Tx\|^2 \ge 0$, the operator $T^*T$ is positive. The continuous functional calculus of the spectral theorem gives a unique positive operator $|T|$ with $|T|^2 = T^*T$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\| |T| x \| = \|Tx\|$ for every vector $x$.
steps.detail: Since $|T|$ is self-adjoint, $\| |T|x \|^2 = \langle |T|^2 x, x\rangle = \langle T^*T x, x\rangle = \|Tx\|^2$. In particular $\ker |T| = \ker T$.

steps.slogan: Define $U$ by $U(|T|x) = Tx$, extend it to the closure, and set it zero elsewhere.
steps.detail: Step 2 makes $|T|x \mapsto Tx$ well defined and isometric on the range of $|T|$, so it extends by continuity to the closed range. On the orthogonal complement $\ker |T| = \ker T$ put $U = 0$; then $U$ is a [partial isometry](c:partial-isometry) with $\ker U = \ker T$ and $U|T| = T$.

steps.slogan: Prove uniqueness by showing $P = |T|$ and $V = U$ for any such factorization.
steps.detail: If $T = VP$, then $V^*V$ is the projection onto $(\ker P)^\perp = \overline{\operatorname{ran} P}$, so $T^*T = PV^*VP = P^2$ and $P = |T|$ by uniqueness of positive square roots. Then $V = U$ on the range of $|T|$, and both vanish on $\ker T$.

concepts.c:bounded-operator: The bounded operator $T$ is the object factored.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Orthogonal complements in $H$ give the zero part of $U$.
concepts.c:positive-square-root: The square root $|T|$ is the positive factor and gives uniqueness.
concepts.c:partial-isometry: The factor $U$ is isometric on one subspace and zero on its complement.
concepts.c:positive-operator: Positivity of $T^*T$ makes its square root exist.

statement: Let $f\colon M \to N$ be a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) of dimensions $m$ and $n$, and let $y \in N$ be a [regular value](c:regular-value) of $f$. Then $Z = f^{-1}(y)$ is empty or an embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $M$ of dimension $m - n$, with [tangent spaces](c:tangent-space) $T_x Z = \ker df_x$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon M \to N$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) between [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) of dimensions $m$ and $n$.
The point $y$ is a [regular value](c:regular-value): $df_x$ is surjective for every $x \in f^{-1}(y)$.

conclusion: $f^{-1}(y)$ is empty or an embedded submanifold of dimension $m - n$ with $T_x f^{-1}(y) = \ker df_x$.

proofs.name: Local submersion form
proofs.slogan: Straighten $f$ near each point of the preimage with the inverse function theorem, so that the preimage becomes a coordinate slice.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $m < n$ no differential is surjective, so $Z$ is empty, and an empty $Z$ needs no argument.

roles.why: Smoothness gives charts and the inverse function theorem.
Surjectivity of $df_x$ makes the completed map invertible at every point of $Z$ and fixes the dimension.

steps.slogan: Write $f$ near a point $x \in Z$ in charts as a map $F$ with surjective derivative.
steps.detail: Choose charts around $x$ and $y$ that send $x$ and $y$ to $0$. Then $f$ becomes a smooth $F\colon W \to \mathbb R^n$ on an open $W \subseteq \mathbb R^m$ with $F(0) = 0$ and $DF(0)$ surjective, so $m \ge n$.

steps.slogan: Complete $F$ to a local diffeomorphism $G$ with the inverse function theorem.
steps.detail: Reorder coordinates so that the first $n$ columns of $DF(0)$ are independent. Then $G(u) = (F(u), u_{n+1}, \dots, u_m)$ has invertible derivative at $0$, so the inverse function theorem makes $G$ a diffeomorphism near $0$.

steps.slogan: Read $Z$ near $x$ as the slice where the first $n$ new coordinates vanish.
steps.detail: In the coordinates $G$, the map $F$ is the projection to the first $n$ coordinates, so $Z$ near $x$ is $\{G_1 = \dots = G_n = 0\}$, an open piece of $\mathbb R^{m-n}$. Such slice charts at every point of $Z$ make it an embedded [submanifold](c:submanifold) of dimension $m - n$.

steps.slogan: Identify $T_x Z$ with $\ker df_x$ by a dimension count.
steps.detail: Since $f$ is constant on $Z$, $df_x$ vanishes on $T_x Z$, so $T_x Z \subseteq \ker df_x$. Both spaces have dimension $m - n$ by step 3 and rank-nullity, so they are equal, which completes the theorem.

concepts.c:smooth-map: The smooth map $f$ is straightened in local coordinates.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Charts of the manifolds turn the problem into one on $\mathbb R^m$.
concepts.c:regular-value: Regularity gives the surjective derivative at every point of $Z$.
concepts.c:submanifold: The preimage is shown to be an embedded submanifold.
concepts.c:tangent-space: The tangent space of $Z$ is identified with $\ker df_x$.

source.note: The standard proof, as in V. Guillemin and A. Pollack, Differential Topology (1974), Chapter 1, Section 4.
